title: An 8–1 hold as energy prices rise ahead of the next wage round
summary: The Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate at 3.75% in April. Huw Pill alone preferred 4%. Consumer price inflation had risen to 3.3% in March, and the forecast implied another rise once household utility bills caught up with wholesale energy costs. The economic issue was the calendar. Fuel prices were already higher, many private wage settlements for 2026 had been agreed before the shock, and rates on borrowing had risen despite the unchanged policy rate. A rate increase could affect future bargaining and pricing long before it could reverse a rise already visible at petrol stations (minutes, paragraphs 2–8 and 13–19).

The inflation forecast was conditional on the energy futures curves over the 15 days to 22 April. Staff projected an average of 3.1% in the second quarter and 3.3% in the third, with a further rise in the fourth. The third-quarter projection was 1.4 percentage points above February’s. Motor fuel and the expected change in the regulated energy price cap accounted for direct effects. Higher production costs would also feed through indirectly, especially to food. A business charging more for a product because its energy bill has risen provides evidence of cost transmission. A repeated change in pricing behaviour or wages after that original increase would show something more persistent (paragraphs 3–6).

The risk lay in what households and firms might learn from another period of conspicuous price rises. Firms told the Bank’s Agents and survey that compressed margins could prompt increases, while weak sales limited their ability to pass costs on. Households had become more sensitive to price news after successive above-target readings. Near-term household expectations might matter for pay demands if they survived until the next negotiating round. Yet inflation at the start of the shock was lower, demand weaker, monetary policy tighter and labour markets looser than in 2022. Precautionary saving and a further rise in unemployment could reduce the pricing power of firms facing precisely those higher costs (paragraphs 6–9).

Three paths illustrated the choice. Scenario A followed futures prices and assumed no extra second-round effects. B and C combined persistently higher energy prices with progressively greater feedback to domestic prices and wages. A severe feedback in C would warrant forceful action. These are conditional pairings, so comparing C with A does not identify the effect of changing energy alone. Nor did members assign shared probabilities. Bailey put most weight on a version of B with somewhat less feedback. Taylor saw a useful comparison with 2011 and judged the more benign outcomes relatively likely. Greene viewed the B feedback as a lower bound. All three voted for the same rate (paragraphs 10–12 and members’ views).

They could agree on a hold partly because funding conditions had already done some of the work. The median respondent to the April Market Participants Survey expected Bank Rate to stay put during 2026, yet the sterling market curve sloped upward. A survey median and a price incorporate uncertainty differently. The minutes explicitly included the effects of risk premia and the asymmetry of possible outcomes in interpreting that gap. That matters to mortgage borrowers, whose offered rate can rise regardless of whether the typical forecaster has changed their central view. It matters differently to a historian trying to reconstruct what the meeting surprised (paragraphs 13–16).

Pill’s dissent centred on the risk of wage and price catch-up in an economy already prone to persistence before the conflict. He judged a modest early increase worthwhile even allowing for employment weakness. Several colleagues entertained tightening under more adverse conditions. Dhingra also allowed for prompt cuts in a durable energy-price reversal, while Mann wanted more evidence on attention to inflation and firms’ pricing power. The eight votes to hold therefore measure agreement on the decision date. They leave considerable dispersion over the next move, the cost of waiting and the evidence that would change a vote (members’ views).

questions.question: Would a higher annual inflation rate change 2027 pay agreements after the 2026 round had largely closed?
questions.detail: Use each firm’s customary bargaining month and the inflation releases available before its settlement. Compare settlements for similar employers negotiating just before and just after a salient price rise, controlling for contracts, labour shortages and minimum-wage changes. A rise limited to firms whose input costs increased would support a different explanation from broad catch-up across employers with little direct exposure.

questions.question: Was the higher borrowing curve already cooling expenditure at a fixed Bank Rate?
questions.detail: Separate borrowers refinancing fixed-rate mortgages soon from otherwise similar borrowers with distant resets. Link their offered rates and spending to sterling swaps, allowing for changes in lenders’ spreads. Record survey expectations separately from market prices. A sharper spending slowdown among households whose debt reset earlier would support an active transmission channel even during a sequence of holds.

questions.question: Would survey measures have detected stronger propagation before published inflation did?
questions.detail: Track the original survey vintages for firms’ own-price plans, margins and wage intentions alongside consumer beliefs. Test whether they forecast price changes outside energy-intensive sectors after controlling for energy and food input costs. A jump in respondents’ headline inflation forecasts alone is a weak signal when the publicly known change to utility tariffs already implies a mechanical increase.
